item.title: AI agents amplify, don’t replace, product judgment
item.description:
Azeem Azhar’s Exponential View piece, “Seven lessons for managing AI agents,” warns that most AI assistants become data‑guzzlers, leaving PMs drowning in metrics instead of steering strategy. The same pattern shows up in Teresa Torres’s Product Talk guide, where teams spend weeks mapping five types of assumptions only to discover they’ve built a feature nobody wants. Meanwhile, a Medium post touting AI agents as a shortcut for PMs glosses over the hidden cost: every “auto‑generated insight” is a new hypothesis that still needs validation. The reality is that AI is reshaping the PM’s workload, not the decision itself – it’s a tool that amplifies the same old bias toward shipping over solving.

The synthesis is simple: AI agents excel at surface‑level pattern detection, but they can’t replace the deep, hypothesis‑driven discovery that underpins successful products. Torres’s assumption‑mapping framework reminds us that every product idea rests on at least five distinct assumptions – desirability, viability, feasibility, usability, and ethics. If an AI agent flags a “high‑impact” metric, the PM’s job is to test which of those five assumptions it actually validates. The Medium hype piece claims AI will cut research cycles by half, yet no evidence shows that teams can skip the pre‑mortem or the continuous discovery rituals that keep those assumptions honest. In short, AI shifts the bottleneck from idea generation to assumption testing.

Lead/Principal PMs should treat AI as a diagnostic instrument, not a decision engine. First, audit every AI‑generated recommendation against the five assumption categories and surface the underlying hypothesis. Second, embed a rapid pre‑mortem step before acting on any AI insight, ensuring ethical and feasibility risks are surfaced early. Third, champion cross‑functional “assumption review” cadences where data scientists, designers, and engineers collectively validate AI signals. By anchoring AI output to rigorous discovery practices, senior leaders keep the product compass pointed at real user needs rather than algorithmic noise.

item.title: AI Tools Speed Docs, Not Decisions
item.description:
Lenny Rachitsky’s latest newsletter shows that AI tools are overdelivering on the low‑hang tasks—drafting PRDs, sketching mockups, polishing emails—but the headline numbers mask a stubborn productivity gap. The survey of a million readers reveals that while PMs report a speedup in document creation, the same cohort still spends the same amount of time wrestling with roadmap alignment and stakeholder buy‑in. That’s the first clue that AI’s real impact is being measured in the wrong places.

SVPG’s "The AI Productivity Paradox" argues that the flood of generative tools has not moved the needle on delivery speed; instead, teams are drowning in more drafts and iterations. A Medium deep‑dive backs this up, showing that commits and PR counts are poor proxies for value because they ignore decision latency—how long it takes to get a feature from idea to launch. Dan Shipper’s contrarian piece flips the script, warning that each automation layer spawns a new coordination overhead, leaving senior leaders with more meetings, not less. The synthesis is clear: AI is a lever, not a magic wand. It accelerates the cheap, repeatable work while leaving the hard, ambiguous decisions untouched, and often amplifies the friction around them.

For Senior PMs, the imperative is to stop chasing tool‑centric metrics and start redesigning the decision pipeline. Map every AI‑generated artifact to a downstream decision point and ask whether it reduces cycle time or merely adds a new hand‑off. Prioritize experiments that couple AI output with explicit stakeholder alignment rituals—brief syncs, decision‑rights matrices, and real‑time impact dashboards. Finally, embed a “cost of coordination” audit into your quarterly reviews; if AI‑driven drafts are inflating meeting load, cut back or re‑tool. In a landscape where every team claims AI‑powered efficiency, the real competitive edge is a disciplined, data‑backed process that turns faster drafts into faster outcomes.

item.title: Experiments Without Outcomes Are Just Noise
item.description:
Reforge’s "Good Experiment, Bad Experiment" makes the uncomfortable point that most product teams treat every hypothesis as an A/B test, even when the underlying question is strategic. The piece shows that half of the experiments run in fast‑moving SaaS firms never surface a clear causal link to a business outcome, turning data collection into a vanity exercise. This mirrors what HBR warned about in "Are Legacy Metrics Derailing Your Transformation?": clinging to familiar dashboards blinds leaders to the real levers of growth, and the cost of chasing stale signals can be measured in missed market windows. Ben Thompson’s "The Copium Wars" adds a cultural layer, describing how hype‑fuelled confidence lets executives double‑down on untested product narratives, while the underlying metrics remain unchanged. The convergence is clear – we’ve built a feedback loop where experiments feed metrics, and metrics justify more experiments, without ever tying back to the outcomes that matter.

The solution isn’t to abandon experimentation; it’s to embed outcome contracts at the start of every hypothesis. A disciplined product team asks: what measurable business shift will we see if this hypothesis holds, and how will we know it’s not noise? Reforge’s framework for “good experiments” becomes a checklist for outcome contracts, while HBR’s critique of legacy dashboards forces us to retire the metrics that no longer serve strategic goals. Stratechery reminds us that the cultural habit of “copium” – comforting self‑deception – thrives when data is shallow. By insisting on a single, outcome‑aligned KPI per experiment, teams cut the noise, reduce the average experiment lifecycle by roughly 30 % (as reported by Reforge’s internal data), and free bandwidth for deeper, cross‑functional problem solving.

Staff PMs sit at the nexus of strategy and execution, wielding influence over roadmaps, engineering cadence, and stakeholder expectations. Your week should start with a audit of every active experiment: map each to a concrete outcome KPI, and kill any that lack it. Next, convene a cross‑team sync to replace legacy dashboards with a living outcome board that surfaces only the metrics tied to current strategic bets. Finally, champion a quarterly “outcome contract review” with senior leadership to ensure that the metrics you track are still the right ones. By turning experiments into outcome‑driven contracts, you’ll stop feeding the copium cycle and start delivering measurable growth.

item.title: Feature Flags Aren’t a Shortcut, They're a Symptom
item.description:
Lenny’s Newsletter’s recent deep‑dive on high‑integrity commitments (SVPG) reminded me why product teams still chase the wrong kind of ownership. Teams that bind themselves to outcomes, not just output, expose the hollow promise of feature flags as a shortcut to product‑market fit.

Feature flags are seductive: they let you ship code behind a toggle, claim you can test in production, and promise rapid iteration. The Medium piece from CodeX correctly notes that they “let you ship code behind a toggle and validate impact in production,” but it glosses over the fact that validation without a clear hypothesis becomes a guessing game. Reforge’s guide to managing marketing work, while not a product playbook, stresses disciplined metric selection – a discipline many flag‑driven experiments lack. The SVPG article on high‑integrity commitments shows that when teams own outcomes, they design experiments with explicit success criteria, not merely “release faster.” The contrarian RocketFlag post doubles down on flags as a silver bullet, ignoring the coordination overhead and the risk of fragmented user experiences. In practice, teams that embed flags without this rigor end up spending weeks untangling broken experiences.

Lead/Principal PMs, you sit at the intersection of strategy, engineering, and go‑to‑market. Stop treating flags as a crutch for missing product sense. Insist on a hypothesis‑first framework, align flag rollouts with measurable North Stars, and embed rollback plans into your delivery contracts. Use flags to protect high‑risk launches, not to replace rigorous discovery. Your influence lies in forcing cross‑functional accountability and ensuring that every toggle is a test of a concrete business outcome, not a convenience feature for engineering.

item.title: Local AI Myths Crumble Under Real Cost Realities
item.description:
Lenny's Newsletter just ran a solo founder’s story where a single developer keeps a 70‑billion‑parameter model humming 24/7 on a home rig – proof that the hardware price curve has finally bent enough for edge AI to leave the lab. The headline‑grabbing setup masks a brutal reality: the electricity bill alone rivals a mid‑size SaaS subscription, and the maintenance overhead demands engineering bandwidth that most product teams simply don’t have.

The hype meets its match in two other corners of the industry. Ben Thompson’s Stratechery piece on IBM’s AI missteps reminds us that even a company with a mainframe moat can’t ignore the economics of scale; cloud providers still deliver superior price‑performance for large‑scale inference. Meanwhile, the All Things Product podcast episode on “Quality of Evidence” argues that any cost‑saving claim must be backed by apples‑to‑apples data, something the Lenny article skirts. The Fungies.io cost breakdown drives the point home: for the average developer, a cloud API remains cheaper over a year of typical usage, and it offers instant upgrades without hardware swaps. The converging evidence says: edge AI is feasible, but it isn’t a free lunch.

Senior PMs, your leverage lies in demanding rigorous TCO models before green‑lighting any on‑premise AI spend. Pull in finance early, quantify electricity, hardware depreciation, and cooling against cloud inference rates, and run a short‑term cloud baseline experiment. Use the results to set guardrails: only when edge latency or privacy requirements clearly outweigh the cost differential should you allocate budget for GPUs. Your roadmap decisions must reflect not just the wow factor of a home‑grown rig, but the hard numbers that keep the business healthy.

item.title: Experiments Without Discipline Drain Teams
item.description:
Reforge’s "Good Experiment, Bad Experiment" cuts through the noise with a single, unforgiving truth: not every test deserves a slot in the roadmap. Over a decade of A/Bs has taught me that teams drown not because data is scarce, but because they lose sight of the hypothesis that justified the test in the first place. The real cost is not a few extra clicks—it’s the erosion of focus that bleeds velocity and morale.

Two recent Product Talk pieces reinforce that warning. In the podcast "Organizational Change is Exhausting," Teresa Torres and Petra Wille map how relentless pivots turn well‑meaning experiments into another source of fatigue, draining energy before any insight surfaces. Their companion "Let's Read Continuous Discovery Habits Together" reminds us that disciplined discovery is the upstream filter that keeps the experiment pipeline healthy. When discovery rituals break, experiments become noisy distractions rather than decision‑enablers, inflating the hidden cost of change‑fatigue that both authors describe.

Staff PMs sit at the crossroads of strategy and execution, wielding enough authority to shape roadmaps while still answering to senior leadership. Your lever is the experiment charter: a concise hypothesis, a single success metric, and a hard budget limit before you click “launch.” Guard your team’s bandwidth by saying no to tests that lack a clear decision point, and institutionalize a bi‑weekly discovery sync to surface high‑impact hypotheses before they become experiments. When a test finally runs, tie its outcome directly to a product decision; otherwise you’re merely adding to the burnout chart that Torres and Wille warned us about.

  • Good Experiment, Bad Experiment — Reforge

item.title: AI Hype Meets Organizational Reality
item.description:
Marty Cagan’s “Great Products, Bad Companies” cuts through the AI‑buzz by reminding us that a brilliant product can’t survive a toxic org. The piece bluntly states, “Great products can’t thrive in bad companies,” and forces product leaders to ask whether their AI ambitions are being built on shaky cultural foundations. It’s a wake‑up call that the most sophisticated model is useless if the team can’t ship, iterate, and learn together.

Two other signals reinforce the same warning. Benedict Evans’ “Predicting AI job exposure” shows that AI will reshape roles, but the impact is uneven and heavily mediated by how firms reorganize – a reminder that technology alone won’t solve talent gaps. Lenny Rachitsky’s “Sonnet 5 review” demonstrates that even a model capable of 64‑generation outputs still falls short of delivering real user value without disciplined product thinking. The synthesis is clear: chasing model metrics while ignoring organizational health yields flash‑in‑the‑pan experiments, not sustainable growth. Companies that double‑down on hype without investing in governance, cross‑team alignment, and clear success criteria are setting themselves up for disappointment.

Lead/Principal PMs sit at the nexus of strategy and execution. Your leverage is the ability to audit cultural readiness before green‑lighting AI work, to demand concrete success metrics that tie model improvements to user outcomes, and to champion the invisible work—process, governance, talent development—that lets AI amplify, not replace, human judgment. Push senior leadership to fund these foundational pieces, map cross‑functional dependencies, and set up rigorous hypothesis‑driven experiments. Only then will AI become a true lever for lasting product impact.

  • Predicting AI job exposure — Benedict Evans

item.title: Open‑Weight LLMs Flip the Cost Equation
item.description:
Lenny Rachitsky’s hands‑on teardown of GLM 5.2 proves the hype about open‑weight models isn’t a gimmick – a 45‑minute autonomous bug‑hunt across a Next.js codebase cost just $3.36, roughly six million tokens. The numbers force a rethink: why should product teams keep paying premium per‑token fees for closed‑source models when a community‑driven alternative can deliver comparable results for pennies?

The shift Ben Thompson describes as the “Inference Shift” in his latest Stratechery column dovetails with the SVPG mantra that “build to learn” trumps “build to ship.” When inference, not training, becomes the dominant cost driver, the economics of experimentation tilt dramatically toward cheap, repeatable loops. Open‑weight models give teams the leverage to run dozens of discovery experiments without blowing the budget, while still retaining the fidelity needed for code‑centric tasks. The old playbook of racing to ship a feature before the market reacts is obsolete; the real competitive edge now lies in iterating at a fraction of the cost and keeping the vendor lock‑in at bay.

For Senior PMs, the action plan is immediate: carve out a token‑budget slice in your sprint budget and treat each $3‑ish AI run as a micro‑experiment you can report on in your sprint review. Pair with engineers to instrument cost‑vs‑value dashboards, then use those numbers to convince stakeholders that a cheap AI probe can surface a critical bug or a design prototype faster than a $10k proprietary API call. Align the sandbox with your OKRs, embed the findings into your roadmap grooming, and make the low‑cost AI results a first‑class artifact when you negotiate scope with leadership.

item.title: AI Agents Elevate, Don't Replace PMs
item.description:
Lenny Rachitsky’s recent piece on designing Claude Code loops makes clear why most teams still drown in manual triage. He shows that even a sophisticated agent needs a human‑crafted schedule and explicit sub‑goals, otherwise it spews output that no one can act on. The same author’s review of Claude Fable 5 reinforces the point: agents can draft specs or even snippets of code, but they hallucinate enough to wreck a sprint if left unchecked. Together with Reforge’s “Moving To Higher Ground” essay, which argues that AI is stripping away low‑value PM chores while inflating the premium on strategic judgment, a pattern emerges – the role isn’t vanishing, it’s being re‑weighted.

The synthesis is simple. Automation is no longer a future promise; it’s already pruning the daily grind of status updates, template‑driven roadmaps, and basic prioritization matrices. Reforge notes that as these chores disappear, the remaining work – setting vision, weighing trade‑offs, and rallying cross‑functional teams – becomes dramatically scarcer and thus more valuable. But the Lenny pieces also warn that agents bring their own failure modes: ambiguous prompts, hidden biases, and outright fabrications. The only way to reap the speed gains without collateral damage is to embed validation loops, treat AI output as a hypothesis, and keep the human in the decision loop. The contrarian view from Wired’s “AI agents won’t replace product managers, they’ll just make them busier” argues that the net workload will rise because managers will spend more time policing bots, but that claim underestimates how disciplined process redesign can flip the equation.

Staff PMs, this is your moment to lead the redesign. Your leverage lies in the intersection of strategy and execution – you can dictate where agents add value and where they must be barred. Start by auditing any recurring, rule‑based task in your team’s cadence and prototype an AI assistant for it, then build a strict validation checklist before any output reaches engineering or leadership. Communicate the experiment’s guardrails clearly, and use the data to champion a scalable, human‑first AI workflow across the org.

item.title: AI Agents Speed Up, But At What Cost?
item.description:
Ankur Goyal’s deep‑dive on Lenny’s newsletter shows Braintrust wiring AI agents into its CI pipeline to trim cycle time. The piece isn’t a techno‑optimist puff; it flags the hidden friction of constantly retraining evals and the inevitable hand‑offs when agents hit edge cases. Goyal’s claim that agents can meaningfully accelerate shipping cycles feels seductive, but the numbers are only half the story.

Across the ecosystem the data are mixed. Kuldeep Paul’s Medium post notes a modest 7.8% lift in overall product velocity when teams adopt agents, but he warns that the gains evaporate once the novelty wears off and teams spend weeks debugging non‑deterministic behavior. ProductTalk’s Momental case study adds a different angle: AI agents excel at surfacing hidden strategy conflicts, yet they also surface a flood of low‑signal alerts that drown product leaders. The emerging consensus is that agents are coordination tools, not silver bullets. The contrarian take from ProductTalk’s “Lessons from 9 AI Product Teams” argues that many experiments end in abandonment because the cost of maintaining agent scaffolding outweighs the marginal speed boost.

Lead/Principal PMs should stop treating AI agents as a shortcut and start treating them as a new stakeholder. Map every agent to a concrete business outcome, allocate dedicated “agent‑maintenance” capacity, and embed clear rollback criteria into your roadmap reviews. When you negotiate with engineering, frame the discussion around “agent reliability %” rather than “feature velocity.” Your influence now lies in policing the trade‑off between short‑term speed and long‑term system health – the real battleground for product excellence.

item.title: AI Agents Add Coordination, Not Magic
item.description:
Lenny Rosen’s latest newsletter riff on AI agents and data integrity cuts through the buzz: the moment you hand a model autonomy, you inherit a new layer of governance that eats headcount, not saves it. He points out that every extra “agent” demands logs, versioning, and human‑in‑the‑loop checks, turning what looks like a productivity boost into a compliance nightmare. The same cautionary tone rings in TechCrunch’s piece “No one knows what the hell an AI agent is,” which frames today’s agentic hype as a marketing mirage rather than a solved problem.

Yet the market narrative is louder. Reload’s $2.275 million raise, reported by TechCrunch, is framed as proof that AI agents can slash coordination overhead by acting as shared‑memory digital workers. New Relic’s launch of an AI‑agent platform and OpenTelemetry tooling is another headline‑grabber, suggesting enterprises are ready to embed agents into their stack. Both stories treat agents as plug‑and‑play solutions, but the underlying reality mirrors Rosen’s warning: you now have to monitor, audit, and orchestrate a fleet of semi‑autonomous services, which multiplies the coordination surface rather than collapsing it.

For Staff and Senior PMs, the takeaway is blunt: stop treating AI agents as a silver bullet for speed. Map the full governance lifecycle before you ship—define logging standards, version control policies, and clear human‑in‑the‑loop hand‑off points. If the net coordination cost outweighs the marginal speed gain, the project belongs in the backlog. In practice, that means a hard stop on any agent rollout that can’t be measured against a concrete reduction in hand‑offs within the first sprint.

item.title: AI Hype Is a Distraction, Not a Differentiator
item.description:
Benedict Evans’ latest Lenny’s Newsletter episode, "A rational conversation on where AI is actually going," cuts through the noise by insisting that AI is a "1997 moment"—big, but bounded. He warns product leaders that the real question isn’t "What percent of my feature can be automated?" but "Is this a task or a job?" The same point is echoed in Mind the Product’s "The 2026 AI product strategy guide: How to plan, budget, and build without buying into the hype," which shows dozens of teams squandering budget on shiny models that never move the needle. Both pieces agree: the AI bandwagon is full of glitter, but the substance that actually moves users and revenue sits elsewhere.

When you stitch these observations together with Ben Thompson’s classic Stratechery essay on product management, a clear pattern emerges. The fundamentals—jobs‑to‑be‑done, risk mitigation, and relentless validation—haven’t changed a hair. AI merely adds a new set of tools to the existing toolbox, not a new playbook. The temptation to re‑brand every roadmap as "AI‑first" is a shortcut that erodes rigor. If you treat AI as a differentiator without a clear ROI, you end up with feature bloat, longer cycles, and a false sense of progress. The smarter move is to lock AI behind a strict hypothesis test: does it shave half a second off a core flow, cut a manual step, or unlock a new market segment? If the answer is no, keep the AI out of the release.

For senior and staff PMs, the implication is stark: stop chasing AI for its own sake and start demanding evidence. Audit every AI‑related initiative against a profit‑or‑customer‑impact metric before green‑lighting. Re‑allocate the saved budget to deeper customer research, experimentation, or improving core experiences. In a landscape where the hype bubble may burst—as Ben Thompson warns in his contrarian "Agents Over Bubbles" piece—your team’s resilience will come from disciplined product thinking, not from riding the next AI fad.

item.title: AI Agents: From Sidekicks to Core Teammates
item.description:
Dan Shipper’s Lenny piece, “The AI paradox: More automation, more humans, more work,” cuts through the hype and reminds us that every new agent we hand a task to creates a fresh coordination problem. He shows the paradox isn’t a glitch; it’s a design flaw that surfaces the instant a PM assumes an agent can operate in a vacuum. The piece forces us to ask: are we swapping one bottleneck for another?

ProductTalk’s “My Team of Agents: How I Get Claude to Do Tasks While I’m Away from the Computer” offers a pragmatic counter‑point. The author stitches Claude‑driven bots into a nightly workflow, but only by defining explicit hand‑offs, clear intent, and a human‑in‑the‑loop for edge cases. Sleekplan’s “Best 10 AI Agents for the Product Manager in 2026” pushes the idea further, listing agents that claim ownership of feedback triage, roadmap drafting, and even customer‑facing communications. The reality sits between these extremes – agents are no longer novelty plugins, they are delegated teammates, but they still need the same governance, prioritisation, and accountability scaffolding we give junior engineers. The sweet spot is a thin layer of human judgement that defines scope, audits output, and reroutes work when the model drifts. Ignoring that layer turns agents into invisible risk generators.

For senior and staff PMs, the implication is crystal clear: stop treating agents as magical shortcuts and start treating them as product‑owned micro‑services. Map every agent to a concrete outcome, embed a review gate, and measure the net reduction in human effort versus the new coordination overhead. Build a governance checklist – scope, hand‑off points, review gates – and apply it to every new agent you introduce. Only then will the promised productivity lift survive the paradox that Shipper warned about, and you’ll have a repeatable framework for scaling AI teammates without drowning in coordination debt.

item.title: AI is for Discovery, Not Deployment
item.description:
SVPG’s Build To Learn framework isn’t just a philosophy—it’s a survival manual for AI teams drowning in hype. When they define learning as "building to test assumptions" and earning as "scaling known solutions", they expose why most AI projects fail. The Rhea’s Factory enzyme breakthrough didn’t come from a bigger model—it came from framing plastic recycling as a discovery problem. This isn’t about tools; it’s about problem selection.

This week’s most important tension is between discovery infrastructure and execution infrastructure. Zartis’ build-buy framework shows the same duality: startups buy AI tools to prove value quickly, enterprises build proprietary systems to own moats. But Benedict Evans’ OpenAI analysis drops the hammer—when the infrastructure itself becomes the product, who’s actually discovering? The compute shortage isn’t a technical problem; it’s a philosophical one. Startups iterating on last year’s features are not building to learn—they’re papering over broken assumptions. Even Lenny’s Newsletter rightly calls out AI hiring tools that inherit human biases, exposing how infrastructure can’t transcend the flawed metrics it’s given.

Staff PMs: Your AI roadmap is invalid if it lacks discovery. If you’re iterating on last year’s features, you’re not building to learn—you’re papering over broken assumptions. The enzymes project shows what’s possible when you treat AI as a discovery partner, not a feature factory. Start with problems that need discovery, not models that need deployment. Ask: What hypothesis requires AI to validate it? What physical or regulatory constraint must we solve for? Your answer will define whether you’re building to learn—or just building to earn.

item.title: AI Workflow Architecture: The End of "Productivity" in PM
item.description:
AgileGenesis’s 2026 AI PM tool rankings drop a bombshell: Jira’s new predictive scheduling engine doesn’t just automate sprints—it redefines them in real time. This isn’t incremental improvement; it’s workflow architecture where AI isn’t a module but the operating system. The data shows teams using these tools aren’t saving time—they’re unlocking capabilities that would have required a 300% headcount increase in 2023. The Idlen.io case studies back this up: one fintech startup replaced its quarterly roadmap with a dynamic, AI-refreshed strategy canvas that adapts to market shifts faster than human PMs can comprehend the changes.

The Planetary Labour automation stats—88% task automation by 2026—aren’t about efficiency gains. They’re a warning for PMs clinging to "manual" workflows as a badge of honor. The real divide isn’t AI vs humans—it’s between teams using AI to model parallel futures and those still "optimizing" workflows that are already obsolete. The Productside analysis of AI workflows reveals the crux: the best PMs in 2026 don’t delegate to AI. They iterate with it, using predictive user clustering tools to discover market segments their own surveys would have missed. This isn’t augmentation. It’s cognitive expansion.

Staff/Senior PMs must stop treating AI integration as a checkbox. The AgileGenesis rankings show the winners aren’t those with the most AI features—they’re the organizations where AI is invisible, embedded so deeply in workflows that distinguishing human from machine decisions becomes meaningless. The homework isn’t about learning prompts—it’s about redesigning roles around AI’s strengths. Those who wait for "the right tool" will find their roadmaps shaped by someone else’s AI.

item.title: AI in Product Management: Separating Hype from Reality
item.description:
Notion shipped its terminal-first agent build flow this week, and Lenny's interview with Max Schoening makes a quiet claim that should land louder: agency is now the bottleneck, not skill. The PMs you envy in 2026 are not the ones who learned six AI tools - they're the ones willing to ship a half-broken prototype on a Tuesday afternoon.

In a world where AI is increasingly capable, the difference between good and great product managers is no longer about skills, but about agency. Agency is the ability to take action, to make decisions, and to drive change. It's the ability to cut through the noise, to prioritize, and to focus on what really matters. As Max Schoening noted in his interview, Notion's design and product lead has been effective in getting designers and PMs to ship code, prototype in the terminal, and launch extremely successful AI products.

So what does this mean for product managers? It means that we need to focus on building our agency, not just our skills. We need to be willing to take risks, to experiment, and to learn from our failures. We need to be able to navigate the complexities of our organizations, to build alliances, and to drive change. As seen in the Notion AI agent build flow, we can use AI to automate tasks and free up time for more strategic work. By doing so, we can increase our agency and become more effective product managers. In short, we need to be able to get things done, even when it's hard. And that's what separates the good product managers from the great ones.
